articles.title: [Just Saying] The next chief justice
articles.summary: Caguioa is known for his disciplined, rule-based approach to law, emphasizing statutory discipline and procedural fidelity, while Leonen advocates for a transformative legal philosophy that…

blocks.text: Caguioa is known for his disciplined, rule-based approach to law, emphasizing statutory discipline and procedural fidelity, while Leonen advocates for a transformative legal philosophy that prioritizes human dignity and social justice

items: Justice Alfredo Benjamin Caguioa and Justice Marvic Leonen are both exceptional candidates for the Chief Justice position in the Philippine Supreme Court, each bringing unique judicial philosophies.

Their contrasting styles create a dynamic environment for legal discourse, with Caguioa focusing on the law's foundational principles and Leonen challenging the court to evolve in response to societal needs.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

For me, it is a toss-up between Justice Alfredo Benjamin Caguioa and Justice Marvic Leonen. Viewing the bench dynamics of the Philippine Supreme Court as an amicus curiae offers a rare window into how Caguioa and Leonen elevate oral arguments through distinctly brilliant judicial intellects.

Whether guided by Leonen’s transformative legal philosophy or anchored by Caguioa’s masterly doctrinal discipline, the Bench would be led by a chief justice capable of commanding immense respect and elevating the standard of Philippine law.

The comparison of Justice Caguioa to Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. captures his sharp, disciplined approach to the law. Holmes was famous for his surgical legal precision, masterly grasp of statutory limits, and an incisive interrogation style that stripped away rhetoric to get straight to core doctrine.

Justice Caguioa brings that same crisp, pragmatic rigor to the en banc, holding counsel strictly accountable to evidentiary standards, civil law foundations, and procedural fidelity with zero tolerance for fluff.

Drawing a parallel between Justice Leonen and Justice William O. Douglas is equally evocative. Douglas was the iconoclastic legal philosopher who viewed constitutional law as a living safeguard for human dignity, marginalized voices, and personal liberty. Justice Leonen reflects that expansive, socio-philosophical ethos.

His questioning during oral arguments routinely forces advocates to confront systemic inequality, historical context, and the broad human impact of legal decisions, yielding jurisprudential insights that push the boundaries of Philippine law.

What makes their presence on the Bench so compelling is how their complementary styles test counsel from every angle: one anchoring the Court in exacting statutory discipline, the other challenging it with transformative constitutional vision — all while remaining distinctly their own jurists shaped by Philippine realities.

In the oral arguments for Baluyot v. Antonio-Baluyot (G.R. No. 257575) — where the Court revisits the issue of whether or not foreign divorce of Filipinos (married to each) should be locally recognized, abandoning the ancient 1939 prohibitory precedent on the matter — that exact contrast in judicial philosophy was on full display.

Justice Leonen’s progressive ethos was unmistakable as he reframed the dispute away from cold codal rigidity and toward lived human realities. By pressing counsel on whether misery could ever serve as the legitimate foundation of a family or state sovereignty, he pushed the Court to treat legal fictions as dynamic instruments designed to serve human dignity rather than perpetuate legal limbo. His questioning characteristically sought to expand constitutional horizons, prioritizing equity and modern social context.

Justice Caguioa’s circumspect, rule-based approach, on the other hand, anchored the deliberation in statutory discipline and structural logic. Rather than dismissing progressive outcomes, Caguioa tests whether a proposed shift can be reconciled with established civil law doctrines, conflicts of law rules, and legislative intent. His willingness to adapt is rarely driven by sentiment; it is unlocked when an advocate demonstrates how a forward-looking interpretation fits cleanly into the broader architecture of the legal system without creating doctrinal chaos.

Together, their dynamic creates an ideal crucible for testing novel legal questions: Leonen asks where the law ought to go to do justice, while Caguioa demands to know precisely how the law can get there without breaking its own foundations.

Reexamining Justice Caguioa through Ateneo Law’s true formation reveals that his approach goes far deeper than mechanical codal adherence — it is anchored in Ateneo’s rich teleological tradition, searching for the spirit of the law (ratio legis) and applying critical analysis to fulfill the law’s underlying purpose.

Justice Caguioa’s judicial craftsmanship reflects this Jesuit Ignatian legal ethos: his circumspection is not cold legalism, but a principled search for purpose, justice, and moral intent within the statutory structure. He tests advocates not simply on the literal text, but on whether their interpretation honors the law’s true spirit without causing institutional chaos.

Justice Leonen, shaped by the UP College of Law’s tradition of critical legal studies and grand constitutionalism, approaches the Bench from a macro-transformative lens. He challenges established doctrine by dissecting power structures, historical inequities, and the human cost of legal rules, treating jurisprudence as a living instrument for social justice.

Where Leonen asks how the law must evolve to reshape society, Caguioa interrogates the law’s spirit to ensure that evolution stays true to its fundamental purpose. Placing either jurist at the helm of the Supreme Court would be a tremendous boon to the Philippine justice system, carrying the genuine potential to usher in the judiciary’s next golden era.
That said, if forced to break what is essentially an intellectual dead heat between two absolute powerhouses of the Bench…well, school pride has to take the wheel!

As a fellow Atenean, if it ever comes down to a tie-breaker, I’d have to shamelessly tip the scale for Justice Caguioa — because bringing a little One Big Fight spirit to the chief justice’s seat is just too good to pass up. – Rappler.com

articles.title: How AI giants could raise the cost of borrowing in Europe
articles.summary: France, Germany and Italy face a volatile bond market as war inflation bites. With US tech giants now issuing billions in AI bonds, they are competing with cash-strapped European governments.

image.caption: AI giants are investing mind-boggling sums in new data centers; those billions are still risingImage: Davide Bonaldo/SOPA Images/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: With more than $1 trillion (€900 billion) pouring into the artificial intelligence (AI) build-out, US tech giants are now competing with governments and companies in Europe for the same investment capital.

Four of the Big Five hyperscalers — Amazon, Google-owner Alphabet, Meta and Oracle — have issued around $250 billion in bonds in dollars since the beginning of 2025, according to a tally of filings to US financial regulators by AI Industry Reviews, an independent platform that evaluates AI tools. They have sold a further €37 billion ($41 billion) of bonds in euros.
Recently, Microsoft — the last of the Big Five to hold back — joined the AI borrowing spree with a $25 billion bond sale, all in dollars.
Next year, Goldman Sachs projects that total new AI hyperscaler bond sales are expected to reach $420 billion. About €60 billion will be issued in euros, according to Dutch bank ING.
Battle for investor capital heats up
That is unwelcome news for European companies and countries like France, Germany and Italy, whose sovereign bond yields have risen sharply in recent months and are already straining public finances.

With public debt at 119% of gross domestic product (GDP) and a deficit still running above 5%, France is already paying a sizable risk premium on its debt. Over the past six months, the yield on French 10-year bonds has climbed from roughly 3.7% to nearly 5%.
The French government's interest bill is set to rise from currently €79 billion to €91 billion next year and over €100 billion by 2028.
Based on these figures alone, France's Finance Ministry needs to find tens of billions of euros in additional cuts, tax hikes, or more borrowing by the end of the decade.
Could France's debt crisis spread across Europe?

In August, economists at the European Central Bank said the euro bond market was adapting well to the presence of AI giants, but warned they "could make it harder for other companies and other economic sectors to access finance."

Writing in a blog post, they also questioned whether the bloc's financial markets can "smoothly handle such large and concentrated debt inflows and warned of a "potential spillover to the sovereign and supranational segment of the bond market."
That means governments and international lenders such as the EU and the European Investment Bank could also end up paying more to borrow.

blocks.caption: AI data centers cost billions and their energy use is putting pressure on power gridsImage: Jordi Boixareu/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: 'Bond abundance' helps drive up yields
Viktor Hjort, global head of credit strategy at the French bank BNP Paribas, described the phenomenon as "bond abundance."

Hjort told DW that the presence of the hyperscalers in the euro bond market is "already high enough to create competition" within the corporate sector and "between corporates and governments for available fixed income funds." These are investment funds that mostly buy bonds, which pay regular interest.

Bond yields jumped again last month, driven by rebounding energy prices linked to the Iran war and France’s political crisis, which Hjort said further revealed the growing competition for capital, as government and company borrowing costs rose together.
Normally, nervous investors move into government bonds during uncertain times, which pushes their borrowing costs down.
AI is much hyped, frequently feared, and possibly overrated
European companies could also feel more pain

Goldman Sachs warned last week that rising interest costs were starting to hurt earnings at European companies. Among firms in the Stoxx 600 — an index of 600 large, mid-sized and small companies across Europe — Goldman found that interest costs as a share of sales have risen by nearly half since 2022.
The bank's analysts said this had cut earnings by more than 5% over the same period.

Factor in the competition from AI bonds, and European firms could now face pressure to cut their investments in new plants, equipment and research, as well as shareholder payouts, to prioritize loan repayments.
Regional governments paying the price for AI
The pressure doesn't stop at national governments. Europe's cities and regions, whose borrowing helps to fund schools, transport and infrastructure, may also feel the effects of the AI boom.

A study for the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development(OECD), published in January, compared local bond markets in Belgium, Germany, Spain, Sweden and Canada. Where AI was spreading fastest, measured by the share of AI-related job vacancies, borrowing costs for cities and regions tended to rise.

"Whereas in the United States, my research has found that AI investments are linked to a lower cost of borrowing for municipalities, the opposite appears to hold in several European countries," the study's co-author, Christos Makridis of Arizona State University's W. P. Carey School of Business, told DW.

While AI bonds are far from the sole cause of Europe's widening fiscal strains, US Big Tech's huge appetite for capital could add further pressure next year, due to the additional billions in new bonds planned.
The irony is that European taxpayers could end up paying more on their own governments' debt, partly to help finance an AI boom across the Atlantic.

articles.title: Sherwin Gatchalian: Senate to cut P8.836B in unsupported infra projects
articles.summary: Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian on Tuesday said the Senate would remove infrastructure projects worth P8.836 billion from the proposed 2027 national budget because of missing documentation from…

blocks.text: PROPOSED 2027 NAT'L BUDGET
Published November 3, 2026 6:14pm

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian on Tuesday said the Senate would remove infrastructure projects worth P8.836 billion from the proposed 2027 national budget because of missing documentation from the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH).
In a statement, Gatchalian said the move followed the disclosure by former DPWH Secretary Vince Dizon that 295 projects had been found to be “non-compliant” in the agency's evaluation.
The evaluation came after Gatchalian flagged eight types of budgetary “red flags” during the DPWH's Senate budget hearing in September.
Gatchalian said more than 62% of the 11,395 infrastructure projects, or 7,107 in total, had at least one major budgetary red flag.
These included projects lacking station numbers and geographical coordinates, lump-sum allocations, overlapping or fragmented projects, and projects with conflicting types of work.

"The Senate is committed unequivocally in weeding out unsubstantiated line items, including those lacking concrete and verifiable technical support, to ensure that every item in the final version is shovel-ready. Unverifiable line items will not receive a single peso of public funding," Gatchalian said.
He said that the Senate would not allocate public funds to projects lacking the necessary supporting documents, saying every peso must be accounted for amid the country's sluggish economic growth.

"Malinaw ang mandato ng Senado, kung walang kaukulang dokumento, walang pondo. Kailangan nating siguruhin na walang puwang ang pang-aabuso sa kaban ng bayan lalo na ngayong mahina ang usad ng ekonomiya at importante ang bawat piso para pasiglahin muli ito," he added.

(The Senate’s mandate is clear: If there are no supporting documents, there will be no funding. We will ensure that there is no room for the abuse of public funds, especially now that the economy is growing slowly and every peso is important in reviving it.)
The People's Budget Coalition (PBC) has flagged more than P1 trillion in potential budgetary “red flags” in the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027.
PBC co-convenor AJ Montesa said P210 billion in the proposed budget constituted “soft pork” in the form of patronage-driven financial assistance.
Another P695 billion was classified as “hard pork,” consisting of politicized infrastructure projects, while P112 billion was identified as “shadow pork,” or unprogrammed appropriations.

Senate finance committee chairperson JV Ejercito earlier committed to inviting civil society organizations (CSOs) to observe the bicameral conference committee deliberations on the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget.

Meanwhile, Senator Panfilo Lacson said the Senate majority bloc supported efforts to remove questionable allocations from the proposed 2027 budget and ensure transparency in the budget-making process.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Burnham denies proposing return to free movement in talks with EU
articles.summary: Prime minister says he is committed to manifesto red lines and ‘public need to be the boss’ on future relationship

blocks.text: Andy Burnham has denied proposing a return of free movement in talks between the UK and EU, saying any decision about the future relationship will be led by the will of the British people.
His comments came as two senior ministers expressed caution about the talk of the UK returning as a full member of the EU or single market and the consequences of a return to free movement.
The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said on Monday she wanted to abide by Labour’s manifesto, which ruled out free movement.

In an interview with ITV, Burnham said he wanted an “honest discussion” about how leaving the EU had affected migration, saying it was replacing temporary migrants from Europe with those from elsewhere who had more dependents and settled for longer.

“I have not proposed freedom of movement coming back,” he said. “I do believe that we should have an honest discussion with people about how immigration has changed since the Brexit vote because the shorter-term migration of people coming from Europe and then going back has been replaced with long-term settlement in bigger numbers, and that was the Boriswave.”

The prime minister said the EU summit in November would cement a deal on food and drink and emissions trading, as well as a youth mobility deal, and discussions would then move on to how the UK could secure a long-term stable deal with the EU, with all options on the table.

A draft text has been circulated among the 27 EU members, suggesting a final deal is close. The Guardian reported that UK ministers were prepared to spend as much as £450m a year to give students from the EU discounted university fees if Brussels allowed the UK access to its Made in Europe industrial programme.

Burnham told ITV that he believed public opinion had shifted on EU membership but he would “not run ahead of public opinion. The public need to be the boss when it comes to whatever happens with Brexit.”
He said for this parliament he was committed to the red lines in Labour’s manifesto, ruling out a return to the customs union, single market or free movement.
Mahmood, who introduced sweeping changes to migration rules in parliament on Monday, said she would not indulge the speculation about freedom of movement.

“What I am keen on is abiding by our manifesto,” she told Sky News. “The prime minister has himself recognised that there were significant issues with the free movement of people, and that should also be part of the debate that we’re going to have as a country about our Brexit settlement and what we do for the future.”

But she said there had been a loss of control over migration post-Brexit and said losing access to EU-wide databases had “had a very significant impact on us and our ability to manage migration into this country”.
Asked if she had been consulted about the prime minister’s comments, she said she had discussed the issue with Burnham.

“I think the prime minister said that he wants to have an open discussion,” she told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme. “I think he’s got a position that actually most of the country can understand, which is we’re 10 years on from Brexit, it’s right that we have an open discussion about the terms on which we left and what the right thing is for our future.

“It’s also been really clear that we are absolutely bound by the terms of our manifesto. We had a manifesto commitment not to reopen in this parliament the question of freedom of movement, and that will not change in this parliament.”

The immigration minister, Anna Turley, told Sky she wanted to prioritise getting more young British people into jobs. “My priority is sorting out the system that we’ve got, getting young people in my constituency into work, making sure we’ve got an immigration system that is not chaotic, that is controlled, that we stop the illegal migration through small boats, that we get a grip on removals,” she said.

articles.title: Jet may have broken apart before Florida crash, officials say, as family named among victims
articles.summary: Adam Robinson, Helen Sharp, and their two children - Emma, four, and Charlie, two - died after the plane nosedived.
articles.byline: Nardine Saad, Kathryn Armstrong, Rachel Flynn

blocks.text: Investigators believe parts of a private jet which crashed in Florida and killed all nine on board may have broken off in the air.
The Learjet 60 was bound for the Bahamas from Austin, Texas when it nosedived into a multi-lane highway and exploded on impact.
A tech entrepreneur and his young family, as well as the 20-year-old copilot, were among those who died on Sunday.

The US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said weather conditions would be a major focus of the investigation, but that it was struggling to access the wreckage due to a huge crater on the road which was formed by the jet in Palm Beach.
The plane crashed on Military Trail, a six-lane road that features businesses and restaurants, at around 12:50 local time.
"The biggest obstacle that we're going to have is recovering the major wreckage from the impacted crater on the roadway," lead investigator Tim Monville said at a news conference on Monday.

The NTSB said the crater, near the entrance to a mobile home park, was partially filled with water because of severe storms. Heavy rainfall and thunderstorms had been reported in the area at the time of the crash.
Debris was scattered across sports fields, businesses and homes in the area.
"We do have some evidence that there was some breakup of the aircraft before impact," the NTSB's Tom Chapman said.
"We may find parts of the aircraft some distance away from the actual impact site."
Officials are also trying to find out whether a cockpit voice recorder was on board at the time of the crash and if it can be recovered.
Flight analysis indicates that the jet was plummeting hundreds of feet per second before crashing.
In air traffic control audio recordings, someone in the cockpit can be heard reporting "moderate turbulence" and that the crew was "managing the ice".
They can then be heard saying the plane was "picking up precipitation" and "we need to climb". Moments later, the same voice said the plane was descending at a rate of 10,000ft (3,048m) per minute.
An emergency was declared and they can be heard yelling "we are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000ft per minute", before saying, "we are going to crash into the ground".

Seven passengers died on board the flight - named in a joint statement as tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson, his wife Helen Sharp, and their two children - Emma, four, and Charlie, two - as well as Rachael Reed, Charmi Fehr and Anita Maria Cetina.
The pilot was named in media reports as Jeffery Gregory, while Nathalia Filgueiras, 20, who earned her pilot's licence when she was 17, was reported to be the copilot.
One man in a car on the ground sustained a leg injury.
Nathalia Filgueiras's mother, Camila Corteleti, confirmed to US media that her daughter had died in the fireball.
Corteleti told the New York Times: "She loved the freedom. It was completely different seeing the world from the top."
In a 2023 interview with a local news affiliate of CBS News, Filgueiras spoke proudly of receiving her pilot's licence while still a senior in high school.
"I like being different than everyone," she said. "Some people think that it's weird that I can fly planes, but I can't drive a car, I mean I can but, a lot of people think it's funny."

A spokesperson for East Coast Jets, where pilot Jeff Gregory used to work, said: "We are deeply saddened to learn that Capt Jeff Gregory was among those who lost their lives in yesterday's tragic aviation accident in Palm Beach."

articles.title: Midterm elections 2026: what time do the polls close today?
articles.summary:
Here’s an hour-by-hour rundown of when polls close around the US, and some of the key races taking place

In the 2026 US midterm cycle, there are 35 Senate seats up for election, 36…

blocks.text: In the 2026 US midterm cycle, there are 35 Senate seats up for election, 36 governors’ races and all 435 seats in the House of Representatives up for grabs. There are also several ballot measures across the country on issues ranging from election administration to abortion access.
Democrats are looking to reclaim control of both chambers of Congress. They’ll need to gain four seats in the Senate to secure a 51-seat majority, and win at least 218 seats to take back the House.

Republicans are fighting hard to maintain their bicameral majority despite mounting national headwinds. They’re contending with a number of unpopular Trump administration policies: an affordability crisis stemming from the Iran war; a deadly immigration crackdown that has seen two American citizens killed by federal agents; a sweeping trade war; and Donald Trump’s own record-low polling.

Already, more than 56 million Americans have cast their early ballots, with millions more expected to vote on 3 November. Here’s an hour-by-hour rundown of when the polls close, and a look at some of the key races we’re watching in each state.
6pm ET – first round of polls start to close
The majority of polls in Indiana and Kentucky will close at this time. But because parts of both states are also in the central time zone, some polling places will remain open until 7pm ET.
7pm ET – polls close in six states, including Florida and Georgia
The next round of poll closings comes in most of Florida, Georgia, most of New Hampshire, South Carolina, Vermont and Virginia.

We’re keeping a close eye on Senate races in several of these states. In Florida, progressive Democrat Angie Nixon is hoping to pull off an upset and unseat Republican incumbent Ashley Moody in one of two special elections this cycle.
Meanwhile in Georgia, Jon Ossoff, a Democrat senator in his first term, is fending off a challenge from the Trump-endorsed congressman Mike Collins.

In South Carolina, Darline Graham, the sister of the late senator Lindsey Graham, is seeking a full term after being appointed by the state’s governor to serve out the remainder of her brother’s term after his death in July. She faces pediatrician and Democratic nominee Annie Andrews.

And in New Hampshire, Republicans are eyeing an opportunity to flip an open Senate seat, with former GOP senator John Sununu challenging congressman Chris Pappas in a race that has become increasingly concerning for Democrats in the campaign’s final stretch.
The remaining polling places open in Indiana and Kentucky will also close at 7pm ET.
7.30pm ET – three more states close polls, including two crucial Senate races
North Carolina, Ohio and West Virginia will all close their polls at 7.30pm ET.

In North Carolina, the open Senate seat is a key pickup opportunity for Democrats, with the state’s former governor, Roy Cooper, facing off against Michael Whatley, the former chair of the Republican National Committee.

And in Ohio, we’ll have the second special Senate election of the 2026 midterms, with former Senator Sherrod Brown seeking a comeback after losing his 2024 race. Brown is attempting to unseat Republican Jon Husted in a contest centered in part on the fight over data centers in the state.
8pm ET – 19 states and DC close their polls

We’ll see a flood of poll closings at 8pm ET. These include Alabama, Connecticut, Delaware, DC, Illinois, most of Kansas, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, most of Michigan, Mississippi, Missouri, New Jersey, most of North Dakota, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, most of South Dakota, Tennessee and most of Texas.

A number of marquee Senate races fall into this wave, including the battle for Michigan’s open Senate seat between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and former Republican congressman Mike Rogers. Holding the Great Lakes state is vital for Democrats, but the race is expected to be close. El-Sayed is leading in many of the recent polls, but is still within the margin of error.
In Maine, we’ll be watching to see whether progressive Troy Jackson can unseat five-term Republican incumbent Susan Collins.

And in Texas, Democrats are betting on James Talarico, the state lawmaker who has surged in the polls, to defeat Ken Paxton, the scandal-plagued Republican attorney general. A Democratic victory would mark the party’s first statewide win in more than 30 years.
Finally, Kansas has emerged as a late-breaking battleground, with Adam Hamilton seeking to unseat Republican Roger Marshall and become the state’s first Democratic senator in nearly a century.
There are also several competitive down-ballot House races in Michigan, New Jersey and Pennsylvania, where Democrats are hoping to flip swing seats won by Republicans in 2024.
At 8.30pm ET, Arkansas’ polls will close.
9pm ET – polls close in ten more states, including Arizona, Iowa and Wisconsin

In Arizona, there are several competitive contests, including the race for the sixth congressional district, where Republican incumbent Juan Ciscomani faces Democrat JoAnna Mendoza, a former US marine.

The state’s race for governor is also one we’re watching. Democratic incumbent Katie Hobbs is seeking a second term, but first must beat congressman Andy Biggs, who won the president’s endorsement in the Republican primary.
In Iowa, the neck-and-neck race for the open Senate seat pits Republican congresswoman Ashley Hinson against Democratic state lawmaker Josh Turek.
The Hawkeye state’s gubernatorial race is also shaping up to be competitive, with Democratic state auditor Rob Sand facing Republican nominee Zach Lahn.

At 9pm ET, polls will also close in Louisiana, Colorado, Minnesota, Nebraska, New Mexico, New York, Wisconsin and Wyoming. Any remaining polling places in North Dakota, South Dakota and Texas will close at this time as well.
10pm ET – polls close in Idaho, Montana, Nevada and Utah
At 10pm ET, we’ll see almost all polls close in Idaho, Montana, Nevada and Utah.

One of the more under-the-radar gubernatorial races we’re watching is in Nevada, where Democratic attorney general Aaron Ford is hoping to unseat Republican governor Joe Lombardo in the Sun Belt battleground that Trump won in 2024.
Many polling places in one Oregon county will also close at 10pm ET.
11pm ET – polls close in California and other west coast states

At 11pm ET, we’ll see polls close in California, where former health secretary Xavier Becerra, a Democrat, is facing Republican Steve Hilton, a former adviser to British prime minister David Cameron, in the race for governor.
Most polls will also close in Oregon, along with all polls in Washington state.

In Washington, two-term Democrat Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, who has frequently broken with her party on key issues, is hopin to hold on to her seat in a district that Trump carried in each of the last three presidential elections.
Midnight ET – final polls close in Alaska and Hawaii
Closing out the night will be Alaska and Hawaii, where most polling places will wrap up voting by midnight ET.

Alaska is also one of Democrats’ key pickup opportunities. Former congresswoman Mary Peltola has led Republican incumbent Dan S Sullivan in recent polls as frustration with the Trump administration has grown and voters contend with soaring energy prices in the wake of the Iran war.

The race has drawn scrutiny from the Trump administration and the president himself, who have accused Peltola and Democrats of recruiting a namesake candidate to siphon votes from Sullivan. The justice department even sought to delay certification if the Trump-backed Sullivan lost, though a federal judge recently rejected that effort. Peltola’s campaign denied recruiting Dan J Sullivan, but a recent New York Times report suggested otherwise.

articles.title: ‘I am deeply sorry’: Craig Silvey pens 9,000-word apology for child porn offences
articles.summary:
The children’s author says he was abused as a child as he begins seven-month sentence for possessing depraved material

  • Get our

blocks.text: The disgraced best-selling author Craig Silvey has revealed he was abused as a child in a 9,000-word apology published after he was jailed for child exploitation offences.

The young adult novelist was sentenced on Monday to seven months’ imprisonment, after being charged in January and subsequently pleading guilty to distributing and possessing depraved child exploitation material.
The 44-year-old writer posted an article on his Substack titled “My Apology”.
He said that throughout his life he had always been able to find the right words, “but articulating the depth of my contrition and the enormity of my remorse feels beyond my aptitude for language”.
“I am guilty of these offences. I am appalled and mortified by my conduct, and I am deeply, profoundly sorry,” he wrote.
“I want to acknowledge that my engagement with this material is reprehensible and indefensible.
“It is re-traumatising to victims, and perpetuates a cycle of harm.”

Silvey, a father of three, said he betrayed the trust of thousands of people across the country, including those who had read his books, many of whom reacted to his offending with “shock, dismay, disgust, concern and disappointment”.

“I am painfully aware of the possible assumption that my offence must have been informed by a horrible and inappropriate attraction, and that my behaviour must then be connected to sinister and ulterior motivations,” he wrote.
“I assure you this is not the case at all.”
Silvey said he had carried a history of “trauma, shame and anxiety” through most of his life.
“As a child, I experienced emotional neglect, violence, and sexual abuse,” he wrote.
Silvey said he suffered a “crisis of mental health and a destructive, despairing breakdown” before he offended.
He was found with numerous sexually explicit photos and videos of children and adults on his laptop and mobile phone when police raided his home in Fremantle.

He also engaged in an online conversation with a person he believed shared his interest in child exploitation material, telling them he preferred boys aged five-plus before adding that “eight was the perfect age”.
“I want to make out with little ones,” the author said in one message.
“I haven’t had any experience, I’m sad to say.
“I’m a bit obsessed.”

Silvey, who has been shortlisted for the Miles Franklin literary award and the International Dublin literary award, is best known for his 2009 coming‑of‑age novel Jasper Jones, which had been considered a modern Australian classic and was adapted into a feature film and several stage productions.
He has also been widely recognised for other books, including Rhubarb, Honeybee – which won the Australian Indie Book Award in 2021 – and the children’s novel Runt, which was also made into a film.

articles.title: Asda appoints former Morrisons boss as chief executive as sales struggle
articles.summary: David Potts to take over immediately, as executive chair Allan Leighton steps back to non-executive strategic role

blocks.text: Asda has appointed the 69-year-old former boss of Morrisons, David Potts, as chief executive with immediate effect as it continues to struggle to lift sales.

The UK’s third largest supermarket said that 73-year-old executive chair Allan Leighton, who has been running the business since 2024, would now step back to a non-executive role focusing on “the long-term strategic agenda for the business”.

Potts, who began his career on the shop floor at Tesco aged 16 and worked at the UK’s biggest supermarket for decades eventually heading its UK business, went on to become chief executive of Morrisons between 2015 and 2023. He left after the supermarket group was taken private by US investment house Clayton, Dubilier & Rice in 2021.

Asda and Morrisons are struggling as they face heavy competition and high levels of debt. Aldi is poised to overtake Asda to become the UK’s third-largest supermarket, with about one percentage point separating them. Asda’s sales fell by 0.5% in the three months to 4 October according to the latest figures from market research group Worldpanel by Numerator despite its efforts to trim prices and improve its ranges and availability of stock.
The appointment of Potts comes after a long search for a chief executive by Asda but is a surprise move as Leighton had indicated he expected to fill the role with an internal candidate.
Leighton said he was “really excited” to appoint Potts.

“Over the last two years, we have stabilised the business and returned it to some growth and begun to establish Asda as ‘more than a supermarket’ through our Formula for Growth strategy. David has an outstanding record in our industry, his experience is exactly what we now require for the next stage of our transformation and beyond and it will be great to work with him,” Leighton said.

Potts said: “Asda has long been a great business, one I’ve admired and traded against over many years. The colleagues are remarkable, some of the most passionate I’ve met. The business has made good progress but significant opportunities remain and I’m delighted and very proud to have been asked by Allan to lead the team.

“Providing value to families across the UK has always been in Asda’s DNA and by making improvements to the shopping trip every week, which customers can experience and feel in their pockets, we will revitalise the business and bring benefits for all our stakeholders, including our 116,296 very hard-working colleagues.
after newsletter promotion
“Christmas is upon us and the business has a clear focus on keeping Asda prices locked low at this important time for our customers. I’m excited to get started.”

articles.title: Could Xi come to Manila? Palace says visit could help settle tension
articles.summary: China has yet to announce who will attend the Nov. 16-18 ASEAN Summit and Related Summits in Manila.

blocks.text: November 3, 2026 | 5:43pm
Chinese President Xi Jinping attends a welcoming ceremony held for the visit of Germany’s President Frank-Walter Steinmeier outside the Great Hall of the People in Beijing on October 30, 2026.
Kai Naito / pool via AFP

MANILA, Philippines — Malacañang said Chinese President Xi Jinping would be welcome at this month’s ASEAN leaders’ summit in Manila as an opportunity to address tensions with the Philippines, although Beijing has yet to confirm whether he will attend.

"It would really be better if China's leadership comes, because it is a better opportunity to talk about whatever rifts there may be and to have the chance to resolve them there," Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said at a briefing Tuesday, November 3 in Filipino.
"That is the very reason for a summit — so that whatever issues there are among the region can be discussed and settled," she said.
Asked whether Marcos had followed through on the invitation he floated last year to Xi, Castro said the Palace did not yet have details and referred the question to the Department of Foreign Affairs.
Beijing yet to name its delegation
The 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits will run from November 16 to 18.
This closes the Philippines' year as chair of the 11-member bloc before Singapore takes over in 2027.
The November summit is the larger of the year's two summits because it brings in dialogue partners such as China, Japan and the United States.
US President Donald Trump is expected to attend.
China has not said who will lead its delegation and the DFA has yet to confirm Xi's attendance.
Beijing traditionally sends its premier to ASEAN summits.

Xi is also due to host the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders' meeting in Shenzhen on November 18 and 19, according to China's foreign ministry, which overlaps with the final day of the ASEAN summit in Manila.
Marcos first raised the idea of a Xi visit in October 2025 when he said he would "certainly invite" Xi to Manila.

“If we get to that point where President Xi will actually consider coming to the Philippines, it would mean that we have made significant progress [on the South China Sea Code of Conduct]. And that would be a great thing," Marcos said at the time.
The Chinese president has not visited Manila since a state visit in November 2018, during the Duterte administration.
China has no set term limits for presidents.
Code talks, strained ties
China claims almost the entire South China Sea, an area that overlaps with the exclusive economic zones of the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia, Brunei and Indonesia.
The code, under formal negotiation between ASEAN and China since 2013, is meant to set rules of behavior in the contested waters rather than settle maritime claims.
Relations between Manila and Beijing have worsened this year, one factor being the continued barbs being traded between China's embassy in Manila and Philippine officials.
On October 19, Lazaro summoned Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan over his remark days earlier that "if we want to use force, we may easily win," telling him it was "provocative and unacceptable."
Marcos said the comment sounded like a threat.

MANILA, Philippines – Remember Villar Land‘s spectacular P1.3-trillion property revaluation that fell apart under scrutiny?

Another company in billionaire Manny Villar‘s business empire has now reported a massive downgrade in property values. On top of that, its sister retailers have nearly P2 billion in rental obligations on the books.

VistaREIT, a real estate investment trust (REIT) which owns 10 malls and two office buildings, disclosed that the value of its investment properties plunged by nearly half (45.5%) to P15.50 billion at end-2025 from P28.45 billion in 2024.

The P12.97-billion valuation loss dragged the company to a P11.46-billion net loss for 2025, a dizzying 330% drop from last year, according to its long-delayed annual report finally made public on Tuesday, November 3.

What does this loss mean? VistaREIT did not actually lose nearly P13 billion in cash, nor did its properties suddenly lose that much rental business. In fact, the company reported a 97% occupancy rate.

The loss came largely from changes in how much its properties are estimated to be worth. Appraisers calculate property values partly by looking at the rental income they are expected to generate in the future, then “discounting” those future earnings to estimate their value back in the present. A discount rate is used to accounts for the time value of money and investment risks. The higher the rate, the less those future earnings are worth today.

For VistaREIT, that rate rose from 8.40% in 2024 to between 10.87% and 11.26% in 2025, cutting the estimated value of its properties. Under the fair-value model, that paper loss is also reflected in reported net income.

Without the property revaluation, VistaREIT said it would have earned P1.45 billion in net income in 2025, slightly higher than the P1.44 billion recorded in 2024 . However, its revenue still fell 18.8% to P2.17 billion, with rental income declining 21.2% to P1.94 billion.

blocks.caption: SEC chief Francis Lim to Villars: No family is too powerful to sue

blocks.text: Changing property valuations are only half of VistaREIT’s story.

Its report shows that the AllValue group — anchor tenants which include AllHome, AllDay, and other Villar-owned retailers — had P1.99 billion in lease receivables excluding future rent escalations at end-2025, up from P1.69 billion in 2024. Including future lease escalations, the figure reached P3.87 billion.

These represent rent owed to VistaREIT but not yet collected. The company described the P1.99-billion balance as “legally enforceable and due and demandable,” although its report does not say how much rent was actually overdue by Villar’s other companies. (READ: Anyare? Villars’ AllHome, AllDay confirm store closures)

Despite the growing rental receivables, VistaREIT has not recorded any expected losses on amounts owed by related companies. It expects to recover the money, partly because its ultimate parent, the Villar family holding company Fine Properties, has offered property holdings and other assets to back those obligations.

“In addition, Fine Properties, Inc, the Company’s ultimate Parent Company, offers appropriate support and makes available its property holdings and other assets in relation to the recoverability of the related party receivables. As such, the Company believes that the related party receivables are recoverable,” read the audited financial statements in its discussion about related party receivables.

The new numbers come at an awkward time for the Villar group, which has been exploring property sales as billions in debt repayments approach. Flagship developer Vista Land reported a 59% drop in 2025 net income amid higher financing costs. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Hate Is a Straight Line in a World of Casual Ableism
articles.summary: Before I even understood what a disability was, I understood what it felt like to be watched.  Growing up with

blocks.text: Before I even understood what a disability was, I understood what it felt like to be watched.

Growing up with my older brother, a person with high-needs autism, public places were almost never neutral. Every sudden twist and turn, or every vocal stim that broke the ambient noise of a restaurant, was met with quiet giggles or exaggerated stares.
Children in school would mimic his bodily stims right in front of me, and some “well-meaning” adults would more often than not pull me aside with unsolicited advice.
“Dapat diyan, pinaparusahan. Hindi dapat hinahayaan na ganyan ‘yan.”
As if his condition was merely a failure of discipline, and that a few hits would cure him. I’ve been told countless times that they probably didn’t mean it, especially the children.
The adults told me that the cruelty was a symptom of either youth or ignorance, something people would outgrow once they encountered awareness and reached maturity.
But years later, in college lecture halls filled with people who supposedly knew better, it was the same.
The laughter hadn’t vanished—it simply achieved a slicker vocabulary.
“Is he acoustic?” (slang for autistic, used as an insult)
“No, he must be r-word.”

I would hear those terms over and over again every time someone acted “unusual” in class. Using internet slang to turn a condition into some sort of clever punchline, and using a slur with so much offensive history as a light joke.
“It’s not that deep. You know what we meant.”
But I would remember the disapproving stares, the whispered comments every time my brother’s pitch went high, and the countless playground arguments I’ve had on his behalf.
It is deep.
Deep enough that despite my fierce, unconditional love for my brother, society had managed to make a child feel shame.
As I grew up, that childhood shame turned into sharp disappointment—in myself, and everyone else. I assumed college would be different. But someone would say ‘acoustic’ and an entire row would laugh.
It taught me a harsher truth. Education, as I learned, does not remove discrimination. It just knows how to make it more socially palatable.

Discrimination isn’t just a schoolyard behavior we grow out of—it follows us straight into adulthood. We see this dynamic play out publicly when the hosts of a podcast made cruel remarks about Joshua Aquino’s autism alongside a joke about Down syndrome. Grown men with popular platforms hide behind the excuses of “banter”, “freedom of speech”, and “impulse control” to reduce disabled people to laughs.

That case wasn’t an isolated lapse of judgment, proven by the way they apologized—using another disorder like ADHD to justify cruel remarks, as if one diagnosis could be borrowed to mock another. The apology treated disability as an alibi, and not as people’s lives. Their response shows just how deeply normalized ableism remains in our country under the guise of content and chismis.

I didn’t read the comments at first when it blew up. I knew I’d get hot-headed, and didn’t trust what I’d type. Anger is something I had to swallow my entire childhood. My sweet brother, who understands none of it, went about his day smiling at every family member while humming. When I finally looked, most people were defending Joshua and condemning the hosts—which I was glad of.
But it didn’t stop me from wondering where that outrage goes when it’s an ordinary kid in public.

Our outrage has a ceiling. We reserve it for physical violence and trending neglect, and then we file everything beneath that—the jokes, the stares, the “non-malicious” microaggressions as harmless. As long as there is no physical harm included, no harm was meant.

However the moment we mock persons with autism, or anyone with a disability, we are comfortable with their pain. When you laugh at someone long enough and stop really seeing them, it makes leaving them out easier.
Obviously, an actual punch isn’t a punchline. Both are not the same act. But they begin from the same decision, one that decided that my brother’s dignity is negotiable.

The jokes make neglect feel normal. And the neglect makes the jokes feel true. That’s how it grows, that’s how it travels. Neglect doesn’t need outright villains, just a crowd who learned early not to look at people’s pain.

Joshua Aquino is easily one of the most recognizable persons with autism in the country, but this didn’t shield him from being ridiculed. If someone as high-profile as him couldn’t escape from being turned into a joke, how about the ordinary day-to-day neurodivergent and disabled Filipinos?

Autism awareness is everywhere. But the thing is, there is a massive difference between knowing that persons with autism exist and actually respecting them. Without accountability, awareness is nothing but hollow posters in a mall where my brother is still stared at.

But this everyday cruelty isn’t just about hurting a person’s feelings. This is about staying complicit while it directly shapes the physical world we build, the media we consume, and the laws we pass. Yes, the laughter inside a classroom and podcast booths eventually hardens into institutional neglect.
Here is what that looks like.

A server questioning my family when we hand them my brother’s PWD card, because he looks ‘normal’ at first glance. So my mother says it out loud every time: he has autism. We explain so there are no further questions, like a guaranteed law needs a witness.

Add the malls with blaring lights and noise, therapy that costs more than a family’s monthly grocery bill, the basic protections under the PWD law that goes unenforced—and a country that makes families prove their need before it honors it.

When podcast hosts, classmates, and lawmakers view persons with autism as punchlines and burdens rather than equal citizens, their basic rights are no longer defaults but rather seen as special favors. And that mindset does not start in government halls; it starts in our chats, the streets, our circles.
Which means, it is ours to change.
Dignity is not something my brother, Joshua Aquino, or anyone, should have to earn by acting “normal” or fitting in quietly into public spaces. It is a non-negotiable human right.
And until we realize that casual cruelty sits on the exact same line as systemic neglect, all of our campaigns and infographics and awareness months will remain nothing but trending buzzwords.
If we truly want inclusion, we must stop separating “harmless” jokes from actual harm.
Hate is a straight line: casual cruelty at one end, systemic neglect at the other, and every step in between leads the same way. And at the end of that line is someone real.

Somewhere in my house as I write this, my brother is humming, smiling at whoever walks in. Trusting the world to be as kind as he is. None of us have earned that trust yet, the least we could do is make it true.
It’s time we step off the line.

articles.title: ‘Mogging’ crowned Collins word of the year
articles.summary:
Bodybuilding slang referring to making someone else look inferior beat entries concerning AI and climate crisis

Mogging – meaning to outperform or outshine someone or something – has been…

blocks.text: Mogging – meaning to outperform or outshine someone or something – has been named Collins’s word of the year 2026.
Announcing the winner in an article for Collins, the copywriter Rachel Quin said the term describes making someone or something look inferior in terms of appearance, confidence or status.
Believed to originate as a shortening of “Amog” (alpha male of the group), the word had first appeared in bodybuilding culture around 2016 before spreading through online communities, Quin said.

By 2026, the expression had entered everyday slang. “Teenagers mog elite athletes, a new video game mogs an old favourite, and your friend’s sourdough mogs the loaf you spent all weekend proving,” Quin said. “Basically, if someone or something has made you look a bit rubbish by comparison, you’ve been mogged.”
Quin said that much of this year’s shortlisted terms felt like “one big mogging contest”, pointing to trends across transport, politics, climate, employment and culture.
In transport, the shortlist features “carspreading”, which describes the tendency of motor manufacturers to produce increasingly longer, wider and heavier vehicles.
Quin said that sport utility vehicles (SUVs) made up more than half of new car sales in 2025, leading to tighter spaces in parking bays and country lanes.

Political terminology was dominated by “Manchesterism,” the philosophy associated with the prime minister, Andy Burnham, that focuses on devolving regional power and combining economic growth with social progress.

Burnham had revived the 19th-century term in a newspaper article in January, prior to replacing Keir Starmer as prime minister in July, Quin said. “His supporters hope the formula that gave Greater Manchester its glow-up can work for the whole country, while his critics are still asking what it actually means.”

Environmental entries include “firewave”, a term coined by researchers at Imperial College London in 2025 to describe multiple wildfires breaking out over a short period during dry spells. Climate conditions also led to the introduction of mandatory “hydration breaks” at every match during the 2026 World Cup across the USA, Mexico and Canada.

In the job market, “ghost job” made the list, referring to positions advertised by employers who have no intention of hiring. Quin said that a recent UK study revealed around a third of advertised roles were ghost jobs, calling recruiter ghosting “a new low”.
Entertainment and lifestyle additions include:

items: Friendslop A term adopted by gamers to describe low-budget, multiplayer indie titles focused on social fun over high-end graphics.
Fricy A portmanteau of “fruity” and “spicy”, reflecting a rise in popular food products such as pineapple and mango hot sauces.
Bixie A hairstyle blending a bob and a pixie cut, recently adopted by figures such as Zendaya, Jessie Buckley, and Helen Mirren;
P(doom) A mathematical shorthand representing the percentage likelihood that artificial intelligence will cause the collapse of human civilisation.

blocks.text: “Look across the shortlist and the pattern is hard to miss,” Quin said, noting that while 2026 had been defined by competition and escalation, the lexicon also reflected how society adapted. “If 2026 has taught us anything, it’s that mogging can take many forms, but some resilience – and a little fun – could be the key to winning through.”

articles.title: P555.75-M fine for motorcycle-taxi app not yet final, says LTFRB
articles.summary: The motorcycle taxi service is disputing a steep fine by transport regulator LTFRB.

blocks.text: November 3, 2026 | 5:23pm
A ride-hailing platform for motorcycles is seeking reconsideration of a P555.75-million LTFRB fine.
Egon69 / Getty Images via Canva Pro

MANILA, Philippines — On-demand motorcycle taxi platform Move It is challenging a P555.75-million fine imposed by the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board for allegedly exceeding its authorized number of motorcycle taxi riders.
The LTFRB said the penalty is not yet final because the platform has filed a motion for reconsideration.
It also refused to disclose further details of its investigation while legal proceedings remain ongoing.
"As such, the decision issued by the LTFRB on the matter is not yet final as there is a pending Motion for Reconsideration filed by the concerned motorcycle taxi platform provider," the board said.
According to the LTFRB, Move It is authorized to have only 17,746 riders but has 55,575 unauthorized rider-partners across Metro Manila, Cebu City and Cagayan de Oro.
The board imposed a fine of P10,000 for each unauthorized rider, bringing the total penalty to P555.75 million.
Move It contests rider count

Move It, a subsidiary of ride-hailing service Grab Philippines, sought reconsideration of the decision, saying it was "working toward a sustainable and adaptive regulatory framework for motorcycle taxis."
The platform argued that rider allocation should account for the flexible nature of gig work, where riders regularly go online and offline depending on their schedules.

"We also want to be clear and transparent about where we stand. MOVE IT views rider allocation as a dynamic measure of live, on-demand supply. The gig economy is built on flexibility, with riders going online and offline throughout the day based on their own schedules," Move It said.
It added that maintaining enough available riders for commuters requires monitoring how many are actively online and ready to accept bookings, particularly during peak hours.

articles.title: Deal finalised to remove Brexit checks on food and animal products
articles.summary: Agreement to ease rules on food imports and exports is now expected to come into force in first quarter of 2028

blocks.text: The EU and the UK have completed their deal to remove Brexit checks on imports and exports of food and animal products ranging from sausages and cheese to leather goods and flowers.

It will prove a boon for British food exporters, for whom trade with Europe has dropped by a third since 2019, and will also mean smaller retailers in the UK such as delicatessens can return to buying smaller batches of cheese and wines, something that became impossible because of the cost of Brexit checks introduced in 2022.

The sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) deal is not expected to be implemented until the first quarter of 2028 after the change in UK prime minister caused a six-month delay to the second EU-UK summit, now due to be held on 20 November.
Last month the National Farmers’ Union said exports of British food to the EU had collapsed by a third since Brexit, with eggs, chicken and potato products worst hit.

Sources said a 200-page text on the post-Brexit food exports had “been settled and there will no further negotiation”. It will be presented to EU ambassadors at a meeting on Wednesday that will discuss the first iteration of a joint statement to be issued by Andy Burnham and EU leaders on 20 November.

The “zero text”, as it is known, also includes chapters on a widely expected youth experience scheme, but this is still being negotiated, and ambassadors are also due to discuss an 11th-hour proposal from the UK over tuition fees for young Europeans to break a deadlock in talks.

Two weeks ago the European Commission was so concerned that the UK would not budge on its insistence that EU students should pay full international fees that the ambassadors discussed “decoupling” the issue and agreeing instead to negotiate on it separately for another six months.

The SPS deal was largely agreed in May and published by the government to allow food producers time to prepare for the change. At the time, the Department for Environment and Rural Affairs said it expected the deal to be implemented in May next year.

Defra has now briefed industry leaders that it may not be implemented until 2028, with a further six-month transition period for a handful of key products such as grains grown this year with fungicides not yet approved in the EU.

The delay is caused by the UK’s need to “dynamically align” British food standards legislation with the EU’s. Although the UK has largely followed EU rules, it has diversified in some areas such as fungicides used to help crops grow in British wet weather.
The legislation is expected to renew controversy over whether the UK is a “rule taker” rather than a “rule maker”, a key issue in Brexit.

Under the proposed framework, retailers in Northern Ireland will no longer have to label products as “not for the EU”, a process criticised in the past by big supermarket chains such as Marks & Spencer.

Talks between British and EU officials began in London earlier this year with the aim of removing much of the Brexit paperwork for both sides. One transport leader told the parliamentary trade select committee that Brexit paperwork had been “pure hell”, with one truck held up for as long as 27 days in Calais simply because it did not have the right certificates for a frozen beef cargo.

articles.title: Sara Duterte defense challenges prosecution evidence in impeachment trial
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte"s defense panel has questioned the admissibility of evidence presented by the prosecution in her impeachment trial, arguing that the documents were neither cited in the…

blocks.text: Vice President Sara Duterte’s defense panel has questioned the admissibility of evidence presented by the prosecution in her impeachment trial, arguing that the documents were neither cited in the Articles of Impeachment nor attached to the original complaints.

In a comment signed by lawyer Karol Grace Oroceo, the defense said the Statements of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALNs) obtained from the Office of the Ombudsman were inadmissible because they were not part of or attached to the impeachment complaints filed before the House of Representatives.

“The 2007-2021 SALNs are inadmissible for lack of relevance to the charges stated in the Articles of Impeachment, as they pertain to a period prior to Respondent’s term as an impeachable officer, without any established connection to the alleged impeachment acts,” the comment stated.
The comment was submitted and received on Oct. 20.

The defense is challenging the admissibility of evidence presented in connection with Article II, the sole remaining charge in the impeachment trial, which accuses Duterte of amassing unexplained wealth disproportionate to her lawful income.
It also accuses her of failing to fully and truthfully disclose her and her husband's assets in their SALNs and of failing to divest from business interests while serving as vice president.
Based on her SALNs, Duterte's declared net worth rose from P7.25 million in 2007, when she entered public office, to P98.656 million in 2025. She was elected as vice president in 2022.
The defense also challenged the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) records, which the prosecution used to show Duterte's alleged financial interests in various companies.

The vice president's defense team argued that the SEC documents covered periods before Duterte became vice president, contained information about corporations unrelated to her, and were supposedly being used to draw mere legal conclusions.

The panel likewise questioned the certification from the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) and the Certificate of Marriage of Duterte and her husband, Manases Carpio, saying the documents were not authenticated by a witness and were not attached to the impeachment complaints.

The defense also challenged records from the Philippine Government Electronic Procurement System (PhilGEPS), which the prosecution had presented to establish business transactions involving companies allegedly linked to Duterte. It described the claims drawn from these records as based on “conjectures and assumptions.”

Duterte's lawyers also disputed the “total value” of firearms allegedly owned by the couple, as reflected in Philippine National Police-Firearms and Explosives Office (PNP-FEO) records, which the prosecution cited as personal properties not declared in Duterte's SALNs. The defense said the valuation was unsupported by evidence or testimony from a competent witness.

The defense further questioned the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) records and reports concerning alleged substantial transfers and remittances from China, drug trafficking and related offenses, saying these lacked evidentiary support or testimony from a competent witness.
It also argued that the bank records were inadmissible because they had been obtained through a “fishing expedition” and had no clear, direct and substantial connection to Article II.

The defense also challenged the Insurance and Investment Company records, which the prosecution presented to show Duterte's alleged investments, as well as the forensic examination report and related electronic documents, arguing that these were based on mere “assumptions or conjectures” without evidentiary support.
It also questioned the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) records, claiming that the Articles of Impeachment contained no specific allegations related to the documents.
In its comment, the defense said the prosecution had also failed to individually identify and authenticate the companies allegedly linked to Duterte.

In disputing the allegations of conflict of interest, the defense pointed out that Duterte had no business interests in Gencorp Industries Inc. during her tenure as vice president and had no affiliation with the Davao City local government unit, PhilHealth Region X or the Overseas Workers Welfare Administration Region IX.

The defense also assailed the forensic report and related electronic documents, describing them as “nothing more than legal conclusions premised on false, erroneous assumptions,” and saying no witness had confirmed the claims.

“The so-called forensic report itself and alleged related electronic documents are further inadmissible, as they violate the absolute confidentiality provision under the Anti-Money Laundering Act,” the comment said.
Under the impeachment rules, the prosecution has 10 days to respond to the defense's comment.
Trial suspension
The impeachment trial is currently suspended to give way to Senate committee deliberations on the proposed 2027 national budget.
The Senate impeachment court is scheduled to reconvene on Nov. 9 at 10 a.m.

Following the decision to drop three Articles of Impeachment, the prosecution will pursue only Article II, which accuses Duterte of failing to fully declare her assets and divest from business interests, raising questions about her unexplained wealth.

Defense lead counsel Sheila Sison earlier said the move would not affect the defense panel's presentation of evidence, stressing that Duterte should still be allowed to address allegations already presented before the impeachment court.— MCG, GMA News
Follow GMA News Online on Facebook for real-time news and developments in the Philippines and around the world.

articles.title: DepEd buying over 170,000 MacBook laptops for P7.4 billion
articles.summary: Apple describes the Department of Education’s purchase as its ‘biggest education deal ever for Mac’

blocks.text: TECHNOLOGY. Public school teachers using MacBook laptops.
Department of Education
Apple describes the Department of Education’s purchase as its ‘biggest education deal ever for Mac’

items: The Department of Education in the Philippines is purchasing 172,654 Apple MacBook Neo laptops for public school teachers and staff.
Each laptop costs approximately P43,000.
This procurement is part of the DepEd Computerization Program.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – The Department of Education (DepEd) is purchasing more than 170,000 Apple MacBook Neo laptops worth a total of P7.4 billion for its public school teachers and staff nationwide.

The DepEd announced on Tuesday, November 3, that it is buying 172,654 MacBook Neo laptops. Public school teachers will get 169,008 of these units, while the remaining 3,646 will be for public school administrative officers.
According to the DepEd, each unit costs approximately P43,000, or P6,900 cheaper than the base model’s Philippine suggested retail price of P49,900. The base model has 256 gigabytes of storage.

The laptops will be distributed from November 2026 to March 2027, and will have a five-year warranty. Previously, the education department’s laptop procurement projects had a standard one-year retail warranty.
“The package includes built-in productivity tools, delivery and logistics, and professional development for recipients,” added the DepEd.
Apple first announced the transaction during its financial results conference call for the 4th quarter of 2026 on Tuesday morning (Manila time).

Apple chief executive officer John Ternus reported in his first quarterly earnings call: “We recently secured our biggest education deal ever for Mac with the Department of Education in the Philippines. They’re going to deploy 170,000 MacBook Neos to teachers and staff.”
Unveiled last March, the MacBook Neo can run up to 16 hours on a single charge.

Apple said in a previous press release: “Powered by A18 Pro, MacBook Neo can fly through everyday tasks…. In fact, it’s up to 50% faster for everyday tasks like web browsing, and up to 3x faster when running on-device AI workloads like applying advanced effects to photos, compared to the bestselling PC with the latest shipping Intel Core Ultra 5.”

In a statement, Education Secretary Sonny Angara said they welcome the participation of the American tech giant in the competitive bidding for the latest project under the DepEd Computerization Program.

“For the longest time, our teachers have carried the heavy personal burden of buying their own laptops or maintaining outdated equipment just to keep up with lesson plans. Under the vision of President Marcos, we are changing the narrative,” Angara said.

“It isn’t just about handing out world-class hardware with five-year warranties; it’s about giving our educators the best tools, backed by robust training so they can focus on what matters most: teaching our children.”
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. promised the delivery of laptops to every public school teacher during his 2025 State of the Nation Address. Teachers’ groups have flagged the long-overdue equipment.
There are around 900,000 public school teachers in the country.

blocks.caption: Laptops vs lapel mics: Teachers’ groups hit Marcos’ unfulfilled SONA promise

blocks.text: The DepEd has yet to specify which schools would receive the latest laptops. But the education department and Apple plan to roll out a series of cluster launches and interactive teacher unboxing sessions across the country.
The DepEd is also collaborating with Apple to launch a co-designed comprehensive training framework called GuroXL.

“In coordination with the National Educators Academy of the Philippines, the training pathway will guide educators toward Apple Teacher Certifications and specialized tech leadership credentials,” the agency explained.
Under the DepEd Computerization Program, contracts have been awarded for 231,725 laptops, so far. Of the figure, 169,008 are MacBook Neo units and 62,717 are Windows-based units.
P10.68 billion was allocated for the program in the 2026 national budget.
For 2027, the DepEd is seeking P13 billion from the Senate to buy over 267,000 laptops. The request came following lower funding in the House of Representatives’ version of the proposed 2027 budget.

The education department’s procurement process has not been without controversy. A 2023 Rappler investigation found that laptops intended for public school teachers during the Duterte administration ended up being sold in retail stores. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Burnham says he has not proposed return to EU freedom of movement – UK politics live
articles.summary:
The prime minister wants an ‘honest discussion’ about how immigration has changed since Brexit

Good morning. In a Today programme interview broadcast this morning at 8.10am, Shabana…

blocks.text: Good morning. In a Today programme interview broadcast this morning at 8.10am, Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, ended by saying this about her plans to tighten the rules that determine when foreign workers and their dependants can get settlement.

double quotation markAs a result of these changes, roughly half a million people who were going to settle at five years are not now going to settle. So on any measure, these are still very significant changes.
She is right, as Libby Brooks explains in her First Edition briefing on the story this morning.

But that does not mean it has not been awkward for Mahmood, who recorded the Today interview, and other interviews, last night. Although her plans amount to a very significant tightening of the indefinite leave to remain (ILR) rules, they are notably less strict than the version she announced last November, which is why they are reasonably being described as a U-turn. In her interviews she had to make two significant concessions.

items: Mahmood appeared to accept that her U-turn could cost billions. She insisted that, compared with doing nothing, her plans will lead to significant savings. But she would not dispute claims that the savings would have been far higher if she had stuck to the 2025 plans. When the BBC’s Iain Watson put it to her that the concessions would in effect cost about £7.5bn, Mahmood just said an impact assessment would be published in due course.
Mahmood refused to deny that she was in effect ordered to change her plans by Andy Burnham.

blocks.text: I will post more from these interviews soon.

Mahmood was also quite interesting on freedom of movement, an issue which has been yanked into the headlines again by an interview that Burnham gave to ITV for a documentary being broadcast tonight. Burnham said:

double quotation markI have not proposed freedom of movement coming back. I do believe that we should have an honest discussion with people about how immigration has changed since the Brexit vote because the shorter-term migration of people coming from Europe and then going back has been replaced with long-term settlement in bigger numbers, and that was the Boriswave … I think public opinion has changed nationally. But I want to be really clear on this issue. I will not run ahead of public opinion. The public need to be the boss when it comes to whatever happens with Brexit.
This is true, and in some respects just old news. Burnham has not made any specific proposals for a new relationship with the EU; he has just opened a debate on this.

But, in opening that debate, Burnham clearly implied that there would be a strong case for fighting the next election on a pledge to take the UK back into the single market, which would involve accepting freedom of movement rules. And Burnham has said that he would like the UK to rejoin the EU in his lifetime, which of course would also mean embracing freedom of movement. The language in the ITV interview implies Burnham is a bit nervous about being seen to have pre-judged where the debate might end up.

Freedom of movement also came up in Mahmood’s interviews. On Sky News, she refused to say what she felt about the UK rejoining the freedom of movement system. And, on the Today programme, she implied that she had not had much warning about Burnham’s decision to open up a debate on this in his speech to Labour’s conference. She also stressed that Labour was “absolutely bound by the terms of our manifesto”, which ruled out single market membership before the next election. She gave the impression that, like John Healey and Jonathan Reynolds, she is not 100% aligned with Burnham’s pro-EU aspirations.
Here is the agenda for the day.
10am: Kemi Badenoch gives a speech on defence at a rally in London.
11.30am: John Healey, the chancellor, takes questions in the Commons.
Noon: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.
After 12.30pm: MPs resume their debate on the budget.

2pm (UK time): Andy Burnham and King Charles attend the opening ceremony for the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm) in Antigua. Later Burnham will be attending a heads of government meeting.

articles.title: Tenerife striker De Miguel dies after on-field collision
articles.summary: Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel dies after suffering an on-field collision during a Spanish second-division match.

blocks.text: Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel has died after the 30-year-old suffered a serious injury during a Spanish second-division match.
The forward suffered head and chest injuries during a match against Andorra on Monday, in a heavy collision with goalkeeper Jesus Owono, who was sent off for his challenge.
De Miguel's condition was described as 'stable but serious' on Monday but his health deteriorated on Tuesday morning, with the Spaniard passing away at 07:00 GMT (08:00 local time).
"Heartbroken, with a lump in our throats and unable to believe this is true, CD Tenerife announces the tragic death of Jesus de Miguel Alameda," a club statement said.

"There are no words of comfort; there is absolutely nothing that can lessen this overwhelming sadness. We stand with his grieving family, with his loved ones, with all of Tenerife who mourn this cruel loss today.

"The family of Jesus de Miguel is grateful for each and every expression of support received, and also requests, from the bottom of their hearts, the utmost respect for their privacy during these terrible times."

Andorra, who are co-owned by former Barcelona defender Gerard Pique, said: "With broken hearts and devastated, we want to send our most sincere condolences to the family of Jesus de Miguel, to all his team-mates, friends, and to CD Tenerife."
Tenerife and Andorra were drawing 2-2 seven minutes into stoppage time when the incident occurred.
Owono ran towards the centre circle to clear a long ball when his knee appeared to collide with De Miguel.
The striker lay motionless on the pitch as medical staff treated him before he was taken by ambulance from Tenerife's Estadio Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez to hospital.
Players from both teams were visibly distressed by the incident, with a number of De Miguel's team-mates in tears.
The referee showed Owono a straight red card before abandoning the match.
Spanish media, including Marca, reported De Miguel suffered a cardiac arrest in the ambulance and was resuscitated by paramedics on the way to hospital.
Tenerife described his condition on Monday night as "serious but stable" but a further update on Tuesday morning said De Miguel's condition had "worsened neurologically".
More to follow.
