image.caption: Iliana Yotova (center) addresses the press after winning the Bulgarian presidential election runoff on Sunday, garnering 57.6% of the voteImage: BGNES

blocks.text: "We are choosing between war and peace," Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev told voters ahead of Sunday's presidential election runoff between incumbent President Iliana Yotova, who opposes military aid to Ukraine and favors dialogue with Russia, and former caretaker Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov, who is regarded as staunchly pro-European and pro-Ukrainian.
With these words, it was clear that Sunday's runoff had turned into a kind of referendum on the country's foreign policy and stance on the war in Ukraine.
Now that the official results are in and it is clear that Iliana Yotova won the election decisively by 57.6% to Gyurov's 39.5%, Radev claims that Bulgarians have chosen peace.
But is it really as simple as all that?
First-round surprise

When the presidential election campaign began in Bulgaria on September 25, there did not seem to be any doubt about the outcome: Iliana Yotova was well ahead in the polls on 44.5%. Gyurov, her main rival, trailed far behind on 26.1%.
Yotova was backed by both the prime minister and his ruling Progressive Bulgaria party, which won an absolute majority in the parliamentary election on April 19.

blocks.caption: Yotova, who succeeded Ruman Radev as president when he stepped down to run for prime minister earlier this year, is the first woman to be elected president of BulgariaImage: Nikolay Doychinov/AFP

blocks.text: But the first round turned out to be much tighter than anticipated.
While Yotova got 34.8% of the vote in the first round, Gyurov was close behind on 31.95%, which meant that a runoff between the two was necessary.
Decisive victory, clear divide
While Yotova won the runoff convincingly, both the campaign and the outcome showed that the Bulgarian electorate is divided.
This division is both generational and geographical, explains Dimitar Ganev, sociologist and political scientist at the Trend market and electoral research agency.

"Younger voters — those aged between 18 and 40 — favor Gyurov. Those over 40 tend to prefer Yotova," Ganev told DW. "It also appears that Gyurov dominates in the capital, Sofia. In smaller regional cities, other towns and villages, Yotova dominates decisively," he said.
'President of peace'
This divide was also evident during the campaign.

blocks.caption: Candidates Andrey Gyurov (left) and Iliana Yotova (right) faced each other in Sunday's presidential election runoffImage: Desislava Kulelieva/BNT

blocks.text: While Andrey Gyurov relied mainly on social media for his campaign, Yotova chose to speak mostly to supporters of Progressive Bulgaria in closed venues.
At such events, the war in Ukraine was always high on the agenda.

"As long as I am president, and if you place your trust in me, not a single Bulgarian soldier will go to Ukraine," Yotova declared at an election rally on October 6 — even though according to the Bulgarian Constitution, only parliament (not the president) has the authority to send troops abroad or declare war.
Throughout the campaign, she referred to her opponents as "warmongers" and described herself as the "president of peace."
"We won because we talked to people about income and about peace," Yotova said after the election.
Russia's war in Ukraine a major campaign issue
In this, she is similar to Prime Minister Rumen Radev.

When it comes to Ukraine, Radev regularly speaks of the need for peace and avoids calling Russia an "aggressor." Both Radev and Yotova oppose military aid to Ukraine and criticize European leaders for not making sufficient efforts to engage with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Gyurov, on the other hand, has sharply criticized Russian aggression in Ukraine.
Appointed caretaker prime minister by Yotova in February, Gyurov in March signed a security cooperation agreement with Ukraine, provoking the disapproval of both Yotova and Radev.
The impact of drone attacks in the Black Sea
In the weeks leading up to the election, several ships in the Black Sea were hit by drones off the Bulgarian coast.

blocks.caption: Bulgaria's former interim Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov is regarded as staunchly pro-European and pro-UkrainianImage: Nikolay Doychinov/AFP

blocks.text: The European Council criticized Russia for the escalation, and the European Parliament called on the EU and its member states "to consider deploying an EU naval operation" there.

Prime Minister Radev, however, was not as equivocal, going no further than summoning the Russian ambassador and stating that "logic suggests that the outcome" of the attacks in the Black Sea "is to the advantage of the Russian Federation."
Just days before the runoff, he noted that "two ships were struck and sunk in Romanian territorial waters" after Romania had held Russia responsible for the attacks in the Black Sea.

"Many people think that once the aggressor is identified, the attacks will stop," he said, downplaying the Kremlin's responsibility. His remarks drew criticism from politicians and the media in Romania.

Yotova also did not name Russia as the perpetrator, instead saying during her campaign that she did not want to see "foreign flags in Bulgaria" — a clear reference to the Ukrainian flag, which has been displayed outside several institutions in Bulgaria as a sign of solidarity with the war-torn country.
How other voters voted

Most opposition parties, including the right-wing conservative GERB led by former long-serving Prime Minister Boyko Borisov, refused to field a candidate for the presidency, which is one reason why turnout on Sunday was less than 30%.

In the first round, the pro-Russian candidate Kostadin Kostadinov from the nationalist Vazrazhdane (Revival) party came third with 12.5% of the vote. According to Dimitar Ganev, around 70% of Vazrazhdane voters backed Yotova in the runoff.
To secure their support, Yotova targeted pro-Russian voters.
How Russian aggression is shaping Bulgaria's presidential election

"Russia is by no means an enemy of Bulgaria," she said in a podcast interview just two days before the runoff, adding "Russia is part of our history, and I very much hope that it will be a key factor in the future security architecture across Europe, including for us."

In the days leading up to the vote, some of her supporters began claiming that the opposition was preparing a "Maidan," a reference to the Ukrainian revolution of 2014 that culminated in the ousting of President Viktor Yanukkovych, who had close ties to Moscow.

"All of Gyurov's lackeys are speaking openly about inevitable protests. They're using prime time to stir up a Maidan. Every single one of them," Sonya Momchilova, who was appointed to the media regulator by Radev, wrote on Facebook on Sunday.
Similar claims were made by both former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban and former Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic ahead of this year's elections in their countries.
Bulgaria in the EU and NATO

"This claim that Ms. Yotova will be a president of peace is directly linked to the incitement of a fear of war," said former Defense Minister Todor Tagarev, who was part of the committee that nominated Andrey Gyurov for president. "Bulgaria will be in a much worse position within Europe and NATO under her leadership," he said during a TV interview.

Dimitar Ganev, on the other hand, sees no threat to Bulgaria's commitment to the EU and NATO. "Over two-thirds of Bulgarians do not question the country's geopolitical orientation, and around two-thirds have a positive attitude towards the EU," he told DW.

But the positions of Radev and Yotova, which many view as ambivalent, mobilized both the pro-European camp and Eurosceptic voters, who, according to Ganev, make up around a third of the country's population.
According to Prime Minister Rumen Radev and President Iliana Yotova, the Bulgarian people chose peace in the presidential election. Nevertheless, the war continues.

articles.title: Supermarket freezers in Belgium and Sweden hit by suspected cyber-attack
articles.summary: One store in Sweden says temperatures for its freezers were set to 50 C (122F).

blocks.text: Dozens of supermarkets in Belgium and Sweden have been hit by a suspected cyber-attack affecting its refrigerators and freezers.
Around 40 Delhaize supermarkets and 15 Carrefour stores were affected in Belgium, while several ICA and Coop shops in Sweden were hit. Thirteen SuperValu shops have also been impacted in Ireland.
Thousands of euros worth of food has had to be thrown away, according to local media reports, with one ICA store in Sweden saying temperatures for its freezers had been set to 50 C (122F).
It is not clear who is behind the attack, which follows a similar incident last month that affected hundreds of French supermarkets.
Delhaize, one of Belgium's biggest supermarket chains, told Belgian media a "computer incident" had occurred overnight at 40 shops.
Carrefour, a French-owned supermarket, said it was "currently analysing" the incident at 15 of its Belgian stores.
Meanwhile, a spokesperson for ICA in Sweden confirmed the incident had affected a "small number of ICA stores operating outside ICA's central network".
"ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the situation," they said.
One of the IVA branches located in Sjöbo, southern Sweden, wrote on social media: "Our refrigerators and freezers have been hacked overnight and they have set the temperature to 50 degrees."
The store was closed earlier but has now reopened to customers.
Seven out of the 800 Coop stores in Sweden are also affected but the "situation is currently contained and under control", the company told the BBC.

articles.title: Democrats condemn Haley Stevens’ ‘betrayal’ following endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers – US politics live
articles.summary:
The latest move has roiled one of the most fiercely contested Senate contests

Some of the people who worked for Stevens’s campaign also reportedly quit following her Rogers…

blocks.text: Democrats condemn Haley Stevens' 'betrayal' following Republican endorsement
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

Democratic politicians have condemned congresswoman Haley Stevens, who lost the Michigan Democratic Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed, over her endorsement of his Republican rival just days before the midterm vote.

Stevens’ extraordinary endorsement of Mike Rogers was the culmination of an escalating feud between the former primary rivals – primarily over support for Israel – that has roiled one of the most fiercely contested Senate contests of the cycle.
As one might expect, top Democrats have been quick to express their outrage at the congresswoman’s “betrayal”.

California governor Gavin Newsom said on the political talkshow 2WAY that Stevens “went another 180 degrees overnight, so something was going on there”. “She’s been successful at taking our eye off the ball and that’s why I understand party leadership condemning it ... This may be curiously the October surprise of sorts,” he added.

Senate majority leader Chuck Schumer also responded negatively to the endorsement. Schumer’s campaign account called it a “despicable betrayal” from Stevens in a statement, but continued to push for unity among Democrats. He said:

double quotation markSenate Democrats are united in our support for Abdul El-Sayed, because we know he will fight for the economic interests of working families in Michigan, unlike Mike Rogers, who is a tool of Donald Trump and billionaire donors. We Democrats equally united in our total revulsion at the racist, Islamophobic, and over-the-top false attacks on Abdul by Republicans. These attacks are evidence of the total bankruptcy of the Republican Party today, who resort to ugly and un-American fearmongering because they have nothing to offer on the problems that concern people today.
Meanwhile, Michigan’s Democratic party chair Curtis Hertel said:

double quotation markHaley Stevens’ decision to campaign with Rogers – a man who has repeatedly sold out Michigan’s working class, wants to pass a national abortion ban, and has pledged to be a loyal vote for Trump’s agenda – shows that she has abandoned everything she claims to care about. We reject the attempts by Stevens and bad-faith actors to divide our party and undermine our momentum, and will not allow these eleventh-hour distractions deter us.

Bernie Sanders joined the controversy, attacking Stevens for what Democrats view as an extraordinary betrayal after Stevens accepted El-Sayed’s narrow victory over her in Michigan’s Democrat senate primaries.

“Rep. Haley Stevens’ staff is right to resign in disgust,” Sanders posted on X. “They understand that the election in Michigan is far more important than Haley’s fragile ego and that all of us must stand together to elect Abdul, defeat Rogers and end the Republican rubber-stamp control of the Senate.”
Zohran Mamdani, the New York City mayor, said Stevens had “betrayed” working class people “by endorsing the very Republican she said she wanted to run against”.
Read our full report here:
In other developments:

items: Donald Trump railed against Democratic US senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed at a campaign event in Iowa Sunday, repeatedly referring to the Michigan progressive as a “jihadist”. The president bashed El-Sayed, a practicing Muslim, in brazenly racist terms, saying that Congress would have to “get a special metal detector for Abdul” if he were elected. “If you vote for this jihadist lunatic that wants to destroy you, you’re crazy,” Trump said.

A judge has dismissed the Donald Trump-backed lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska’s US Senate race if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses. Trump said on 23 October that he had ordered the justice department to file the lawsuit in a move that voting rights experts called an “unprecedented intervention” by the federal government with control of Congress in the balance.

Democratic US Senator Chris Murphy has been hospitalized after suffering a stroke. Murphy, 53, started feeling numbness in his arm while attending his son’s hockey game on Saturday, according to the Connecticut senator’s chief of staff, Allison Herwitt. A hospital visit confirmed that Murphy had experienced a stroke.

articles.title: Her neighbour built a garden suite. She calls it a 'watchtower' over her Toronto backyard
articles.summary: Fed up with what she calls a violation of her backyard privacy, an East York woman is going public with her campaign to have new garden suites limited to just one storey.

blocks.text: Toronto
Fed up with what she calls a violation of her backyard privacy, an East York woman is going public with her campaign to have new garden suites limited to just one storey.
East York homeowner calls for limit for garden suites to be 1 storey high
'I lost all privacy': Toronto woman speaks out over neighbour's 2-storey garden suite
An East York homeowner is going public with her campaign to change the city's rules governing garden suites after what she calls a violation of her backyard privacy.

Sandy Chambers, who lives in the Danforth-Greenwood area, says this past summer she returned from a one-week vacation to find a six-metre-high, two-storey building with a picture window, looming over her back fence.
"After you get past the shock there's a little bit of anger," she said. "I lost all privacy in my yard, I stopped using my yard."
"It fired me up."
In response, she planted trees across the back of her yard, and erected a large screen on a backyard shed, which blocks the view from the neighbours’ new picture window.
In 2022, the updated planning rules to allow homeowners to build garden suites on their properties with fewer city restrictions. (Michael Smee/CBC)

She also ordered dozens of lawn signs that read "Save Our Neighbourhoods. No 2-storey Garden Suites Without a Say." An online petition that she started also appears to be gaining traction, she says, so far garnering about 80 signatures.
CBC Toronto tried to speak with the homeowners but no one answered a knock at the door Thursday.
One of the people who is displaying one of those signs on her front lawn is Rosanna Manarin, who lives next door to the house that installed the garden suite.
She says she was shocked at how completely her light and privacy were limited by the new build.
"I understand the city’s need for density, but what is now sitting next door to me is a watchtower," she told CBC Toronto.
Rosanna Manarin, who has lived in the same house for 25 years, says the emergence of a two-storey garden suite overshadowing her yard this past summer was a shock. (Michael Smee/CBC)
“Your oasis is completely gone.”
New planning rules introduced to ease housing issues
Technically, the homeowners are within their rights under new city rules that govern the construction of garden suites.
Garden suites are self-contained, detached units often built in backyards and not connected to a public lane, according to the city of Toronto's website.

In 2022, the city updated planning rules to allow homeowners to build garden suites on their properties with fewer city restrictions. The idea, known as gentle infill housing, was first floated as a way to help ease the city’s housing crunch.

Instead of requiring a zoning change — which would have meant an opportunity for public discussion about the new build — property owners are now only required to apply for a building permit to put up structures such as garden suites and multiplexes.

items: This couple says they are paying the price of Toronto's housing push

blocks.text: The new process doesn't include an opportunity for public input, as long as the plan doesn’t require any variances — smaller setbacks, for instance.

Numbers from the city show the public has reacted enthusiastically. In 2022, the first year that garden suites were allowed without expensive and time-consuming rezoning applications, just 34 building permits were issued. By 2025, that number had risen to a total of 361.
Staff say so far, 627 have been built while another 755 are under construction.
But there have also been complaints.
Garden suites a 'turn off' for buyers: real estate broker
The city does not track criticisms for the initiative, but anecdotally, real estate experts say they’re hearing from unhappy homeowners.
Real estate broker Justin Bregman says potential buyers he’s encountered are not enthusiastic about the lack of light and privacy that some garden suites bring to a neighbourhood.
In terms of resale value, "It’s a turn off," he says.
"If all of a sudden there’s a two-storey, or a 20-foot (six-metre) high [building] that’s completely blocking your backyard, that absolutely is going to affect value."
City staff did not answer directly when asked to comment on Chambers’ drive to have garden suites limited to just one storey as-of-right — meaning without rezoning or input from neighbours.

In an email to CBC Toronto, staff wrote: "The City of Toronto recognizes that new construction can raise concerns for neighbouring property owners, including concerns related to privacy, sunlight and construction impacts," the email states.
"While these concerns are understandable…these concerns do not, on their own, provide a basis to withhold a building permit" if the project complies with the provincial building code.

items: Alberta government to force Edmonton to change infill rules

blocks.text: Toronto real estate lawyer Bob Aaron points out that backyard privacy is never guaranteed in an urban neighbourhood.
Garden suites aside, most people with a two storey house can see into a neighbour’s yard.
"Frankly there is no right to privacy from neighbouring properties looking into your property in Canadian law," he said.
"That’s the joy of urban living."

articles.title: Merz says next German president 'must be a woman' — report
articles.summary: German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier's second term is due to end in March next year. Meanwhile, Merz has called for 'digital sovereignty' in the era of AI. Follow DW for more
articles.byline: Natalie Muller, Matt Ford, Timothy Jones

image.caption: Germany's federal president is the country's official head of state, as opposed to the chancellor, who is the head of the government [FILE: Jul 29, 2026]Image: Markus Schreiber/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: November 2, 2026
Merz says next German president 'must be a woman'
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has spoken out in favor of having a woman succeed Frank-Walter Steinmeier as Germany's president.

"I will propose a consensus candidate to the party, a candidate from the political center," Merz said at a non-public meeting of local Christian Democratic Union (CDU) chairs in Berlin, participants told the German DPA news agency.
"I am firm in my belief that it must be a woman," he reportedly added.
Germany's federal president is the country's official head of state, as opposed to the chancellor, who is the head of the government.
Current incumbent Steinmeier, a former Social Democrat (SPD) foreign minister, became president in 2017 and his second term will end in March 2027.
Bavarian premier Markus Söder recently proposed Ilse Aigner from his Christian Social Union (CSU), the CDU's Bavarian sister party.

But the CDU itself may propose an alternative candidate from within its own ranks, with current parliamentary speaker Julia Klöckner, Families Minister Karin Prien and former CDU leader and Defense Minister Annegret Kramp-Karrenbauer all having been mentioned.
The CDU's top leadership is expected to propose a candidate on November 9.
